## Chapter 3: History and Application of Six Sigma

### The Development of Statistical Process Control

Six Sigma applies statistics to define, measure, analyze, verify, and control processes. In fact, Six Sigma teams generally use methodologies known as DMAIC or DMADV to make improvements and develop controls for processes. DMAIC stands for Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control. These are the five phases of a Six Sigma project to improve an already-existing process. When developing a new process, teams use DMADV, which stands for Define, Measure, Analyze, Design, and Verify. Both methods are discussed in Chapter 33, and PART IV provides in-depth information on each DMAIC phase.

The roots of statistical process control, which provide the backbone of Six Sigma methods, began with Carl Friedrich Gauss's development of the normal curve in the 19th century. We know today that the normal curve is just one of several possible probability distribution models. It's perhaps the most widely used model, and the other models developed out of the normal curve. Probability distribution models are discussed in later statistics chapters.

*Figure: The Normal Curve (normal distribution / "bell curve").*

In the early 20th century, statistical process control got another major boost thanks to the contributions of an engineer and scholar named Walter Shewhart. Shewhart's contributions to quality are numerous, but two specific ideas stand out. First, Shewhart was the first person to closely tie the sigma level to quality. He defined a process that needs correction as one operating at three sigma. If you go back to Chapter 2 and the theoretical Amazon example, the cost difference between four sigma and three sigma is over $78 million; by comparison, the difference between five and four sigma is only about $7.6 million. Since errors and costs increase exponentially as the sigma level drops, Shewhart's definition has very practical business applications. Although Six Sigma as a method seeks to get closer and closer to fewer than 3.4 defects per million opportunities (dpmo), it's also true that, if a process's quality declines as it approaches three sigma, the costs associated with errors rise substantially.

Second, Shewhart is considered the father of control charts. Control charts, covered in depth in the advanced statistics chapters, are a critical component of statistical process control that lets organizations sustain improved performance after a Six Sigma initiative. At a time when scholars were writing about the theoretical application of statistics across a growing number of fields, Shewhart developed ways to apply those concepts specifically to manufacturing and industrial processes.

Around the same time, W. Edwards Deming was working for the U.S. Department of Agriculture. A physicist and mathematician, Deming was responsible for teaching graduate courses at the agency and arranged for Shewhart to lecture there. Later, Deming carried Shewhart's statistical concepts to the United States Census Bureau, applying his theories outside an industrial or manufacturing setting, possibly for the first time.

One of Deming's ideas is called the PDCA cycle, or plan-do-check-act cycle. The idea is that improvement comes when you recognize there's a need for change and make a plan to create the improvement. Then you do something by testing your ideas. Using the test results, you check whether your improvements are working. Then you act, carrying your improvements into a production environment or expanding the improvements beyond the test setting. The fact that PDCA is a cycle means it never ends; there are always improvements to be made. This is a core Six Sigma principle.

After World War II, Deming worked in Japan on behalf of the United States government in several roles. While in postwar Japan, Deming made friends with statisticians and convinced at least one notable engineer that statistical process control was relevant to Japan's need to drastically boost economic and production performance to overcome the war's damage. In the end, Deming became a valuable teacher and consultant to manufacturing companies in Japan, planting the ideas and concepts that would soon become the Toyota Production System, or Lean Six Sigma.

### Continuous Process Improvement: Toyota and Lean

Deming's teachings and the Japanese industry's need to achieve a successful recovery after a catastrophic war combined to bear fruit at Toyota. Toyota's leadership had already been considering quality concepts before World War II, but improved performance and efficiency became a more critical goal given the nature of Japan's economy and resources in the 1940s and 1950s. Borrowing manufacturing ideas attributed to Henry Ford, Toyota's leaders applied statistics and new quality concepts to build a system they believed would increase production and allow for variable products, while cutting costs and ensuring quality.

Several individuals were instrumental in the final development of the Toyota Production System. They built into the process automated machinery, quality controls to prevent defects from occurring, and efficiency tools that hadn't yet been applied with this much detail and consistency. One man, Kiichiro Toyoda, had prior factory experience. In earlier jobs, he added efficiencies to processes at textile mills through conveyor belts and other automated systems. Toyoda introduced the same concepts into certain lines of Toyota's manufacturing process. Later, Eiji Toyoda and Taiichi Ohno introduced concepts known as Just-in-Time and jidoka, which are the pillars of the Toyota Production System.

The principles that drove Toyota's system, and later formed the foundation of Lean Process Management or Lean Six Sigma, include:

- Defining customer values
- Identifying the value stream for customer needs and wants
- Identifying waste in the process
- Creating a continuous process flow
- Continuously working to reduce the number of steps and the time needed to achieve customer satisfaction

Lean management is deeply concerned with eliminating waste from any process. Waste increases the cost and time spent on a process, making it undesirable in any form.

> **What Is Jidoka?**
> Jidoka is a principle that builds defect control into a business process. Instead of identifying defects at the end of the production line and trying to trace the errors back to their source, jidoka requires a process to stop as soon as errors are detected, so improvements or problem-solving can happen immediately. For jidoka to work correctly, machines are generally equipped to recognize bad outcomes from good ones; machines are also equipped with some kind of notification to prompt human interaction in the process when something goes wrong.
>

### Motorola's Focus on Defects

Although Six Sigma's foundation was laid in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it wasn't until the mid-1980s that these concepts succeeded on a large scale in the United States. Decades after Toyota developed its system, engineers at Motorola began questioning the effectiveness of their quality management programs. These questions first arose after a Japanese company took over one of Motorola's television factories. By applying Lean concepts, the new company went on to manufacture televisions with 1/20th the number of defects of Motorola's own sets.

At the time, Motorola's departments measured defects as a ratio to a thousand opportunities. Bob Galvin, Motorola's CEO, issued a challenge to his team. He wanted to see an improvement in quality and output — not just any improvement; he wanted a tenfold improvement within half a decade. Engineer Bill Smith and a new addition to the Motorola team — Dr. Mikel Harry — started working on the problem.

The team realized that measuring errors against a thousand opportunities didn't provide the level of detail needed for genuine statistical process control. Instead, the engineers wanted to measure defects against a million opportunities. We know sigma levels had already been defined, and the idea of using sigma levels as a quality measure started with Shewhart. It wasn't a big leap for the Motorola engineers to go from their desire for more precise data to the basic concepts of Six Sigma as a goal and methodology.

Over the following two decades, Motorola worked to refine its Six Sigma methodology, getting positive results along the way. Beyond the statistical tools, the team built a step-by-step process by which any team — in nearly any industry — could achieve gains and improvements. For the first time, this kind of statistical process control was taken out of the large-scale manufacturing environment, company-wide. Motorola applied the method to customer service, engineering, and technical support. It used the process to build a collaborative environment among stakeholders inside and outside the organization. It was a huge success; according to Motorola, the company saved over $16 billion as a result of continuous process improvement initiatives over 12 years.⁵

Motorola did more than improve its own systems and products. Galvin directed his team to share Six Sigma with the world. Motorola and its team published papers and books on the Six Sigma method and rolled out efforts to train others. In doing so, they created a statistically grounded methodology that could be taught and implemented at any organization or in any industry.

⁵ "The History of Six Sigma," iSixSigma.

### ABB, Allied Signal, and General Electric

After leaving Motorola, Dr. Harry joined Asea Brown Boveri. At ABB, Harry worked with Richard Schroeder, who would also become a Six Sigma champion. In fact, the two men later co-founded the Six Sigma Academy. At ABB, Harry landed on a core idea in Six Sigma's evolution: business, or profit, in a sense came before quality. Quality was, in fact, a driver of the business. Customers didn't buy if quality was poor. Since the individuals with the power to decide in favor of Six Sigma initiatives were highly motivated by financial results, Harry built financial tactics into the Six Sigma methodology. For the first time, the method focused on the bottom line as the primary goal, with other concerns and objectives flowing from finance-driven goals.

In 1993, both Schroeder and Harry changed jobs, joining the Allied Signal team. Allied Signal's CEO at the time was Larry Bossidy. He was interested in Six Sigma, but realized executives and other senior leaders faced knowledge barriers when trying to interact and collaborate with analysts, process engineers, and Six Sigma specialists. Bossidy suggested a company's leadership needed to be well versed in Six Sigma in order to pick the right projects for success and back those projects company-wide to ensure success.

Harry, sometimes called the father of Six Sigma, created a system for educating executive leaders. Together with others at Allied Signal, he developed systems that let Six Sigma be effectively deployed by leadership across the whole organization.

Around the same time, GE CEO Jack Welch entered the Six Sigma arena. Before encountering Six Sigma, Welch had stated he wasn't in favor of quality measures. He had previously criticized quality programs as heavy-handed approaches that delivered little in terms of results. Welch invited Larry Bossidy to speak at a GE corporate meeting in 1995. He also requested an analysis of the benefits of implementing Six Sigma at GE. At the time, GE operated between three and four sigma. The potential savings if the company reached six sigma were enormous; estimates ran from $7 to $10 billion.⁶

Welch is known as a Six Sigma champion not because he made a significant contribution to developing statistical process controls or Six Sigma's toolset, but because he demonstrated exactly how leaders should approach Six Sigma. He also made GE a historically successful Six Sigma organization by tying Six Sigma goals to employee reward structures. Employees were no longer paid based solely on financial performance factors; they were also evaluated based on Six Sigma performance. Suddenly, employees at every level had a personal reason to engage with continuous process improvement, and employees and managers received the Six Sigma training needed to succeed.

⁶ "The Evolution of Six Sigma," PQA.net.

### Six Sigma's Continued Growth

After the success of corporations like GE and Motorola, companies across the country rushed to implement Six Sigma. Unfortunately, in the rush to implement the process, many organizations executed the improvements poorly or failed to gain a proper understanding of statistical process control before moving forward with improvements. Although Six Sigma methods have been used by organizations to achieve savings and efficiencies of millions — even billions — some companies were left with a bitter taste about the process. That bitter taste resulted in the following misconceptions and myths that are still prevalent today across many industries:

- **Six Sigma cares exclusively about metrics and ignores common sense.** The opposite is actually true: Six Sigma often starts with traditional common-sense ideas, frequently arrived at through brainstorming, and validates those assumptions with data. There are two reasons behind this myth. First, managers and others who are used to making decisions without being questioned suddenly get questioned in a Six Sigma setting. Not only are they questioned, but sometimes hard data proves them wrong. Second, in some cases, data is misused to support conclusions that run counter to common sense or tradition. When those conclusions turn out flawed, it's easy to blame the Six Sigma process when, in fact, there's a lack of proper understanding of the statistical theories involved.
- **Six Sigma is too expensive.** Although rolling out Six Sigma company-wide can be expensive up front, partly due to training needs, slowly working the concepts into a company often costs very little over the long term. Organizations need to balance how they adopt Six Sigma against budget concerns — but, when implemented correctly, Six Sigma generally generates savings that far outweigh its initial investment.
- **Six Sigma can solve anything.** On the opposite end from the skeptics are Six Sigma enthusiasts who believe they can apply the method as a cure-all for any problem. Although Six Sigma can be applied to any process problem, it isn't always relevant to culture or people problems. If morale issues or other human-resources problems are at the root of an issue, statistics can't help. However, if morale is low because a process is hard to work with or performs poorly, Six Sigma can be used to improve the process, thereby improving morale.

### Applying Six Sigma Knowledge

Six Sigma is applied through a controlled process of project selection and management. Once areas of concern are identified, leaders generally turn to analysts, Six Sigma specialists, and subject-matter experts for cost-benefit analyses. Six Sigma teams try to quantify how problematic a process is (by calculating the sigma level, defect costs, downtime, and other metrics) and how much it would cost to solve the problem. Problems are then prioritized according to severity and the organization's ability to solve the issue. Teams start working through the priority list, returning to the analysis periodically to make sure the list hasn't changed. Most of this book covers the methods by which teams identify and solve problems using Six Sigma.

### Six Sigma Certification Levels

Holding a Six Sigma certification proves an individual has demonstrated practical applications and knowledge of Six Sigma. Some organizations offer in-house certification processes. Most people pursue certification by enrolling in an online or in-person Six Sigma training course. Most organizations that offer Six Sigma education also offer a path to certification. Certification courses are available at various levels; Six Sigma levels are differentiated by belt level.

#### White Belt

A professional certified as a Six Sigma White Belt is familiar with the basic principles of the Six Sigma methodology, though they're not always regular members of process improvement teams. White belt training is a good introduction to Six Sigma for support staff within an organization and can provide the information needed to understand why project teams do what they do. The training lets employees review project processes, understand information presented at milestone meetings, and better participate in project selection processes. White belt training can also be used across every level of staff when organizations are trying to build a Six Sigma culture. It's worth noting that White Belt training generally provides only a very basic introduction and overview of Six Sigma, so much so that not every Six Sigma professional recognizes it as a genuine Six Sigma certification.

#### Yellow Belt

A yellow belt certification is a step up from white belt: it's still considered a basic introduction to Six Sigma concepts, but a yellow belt learns basic information about the DMAIC method often used to improve processes. The following concepts are commonly included in Six Sigma yellow belt training:

- Roles in Six Sigma
- Team development and management
- Basic quality tools, like Pareto charts, run charts, scatter diagrams, and histograms
- Common Six Sigma metrics
- Data collection
- Measurement system analysis
- Root cause analysis
- An introduction to hypothesis testing

At the yellow belt level, training generally focuses on understanding the overall methodology and basic data collection. Yellow belts don't need to know how to run hypothesis tests, but should understand the language of hypothesis testing and the conclusions drawn from such tests. Yellow belts tend to be employees who need to know about the overall process and the reason for implementing it.

#### Green Belt

Certified green belts work within Six Sigma teams, generally under the supervision of a black belt or master black belt. In some cases, green belts might lead or run smaller projects on their own. Green belts generally have intermediate statistical analysis capabilities; they can handle data and analysis issues, help black belts apply Six Sigma tools to a project, or teach others in the organization about the overall Six Sigma methodology.

Green belts might be mid-level managers, business analysts, project managers, and others who have reason to regularly engage with process improvement initiatives, but who might not be full-time Six Sigma specialists within an organization. Green belts are sometimes considered the "worker bees" of the Six Sigma methodology, since they carry out most of the statistical data collection and analysis under the supervision of certified black belts.

The following concepts are commonly included in Green Belt training:

- Everything listed for the yellow belt certification
- Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA)
- Project and team management
- Probability and the Central Limit Theorem
- Statistical distributions
- Descriptive statistics
- How to run basic hypothesis tests
- Waste elimination and Kaizen
- Basic control charts

#### Black Belt

A certified Six Sigma Black Belt generally acts as a project leader on process improvement projects. They might also serve in management, analysis, or planning roles company-wide. The common minimum requirements for black belt certification include everything listed for yellow and green belts, plus:

- Advanced project and team management skills
- Knowledge of Six Sigma's extensive list of brainstorming and design tools
- Intermediate to advanced statistics
- An understanding of other process improvement and quality programs, including Lean and Total Quality Management
- The ability to design processes
- Advanced process diagramming capabilities, including flowcharts and value stream maps
- Use of software to run analyses, like Excel or Minitab

#### Master Black Belt

A Master Black Belt is the highest certification level achievable in Six Sigma. Within a business organization, Master Black Belts generally manage Black Belts and Green Belts, consult on especially difficult project issues, offer advice and education on challenging statistical concepts, and train others in the Six Sigma methodology.

#### Certification Exams

Most certification programs require individuals to pass an exam for certification; some also require green belt and black belt candidates to demonstrate their knowledge in the form of Six Sigma project experience.

If an exam is required for white or yellow belt certification, it's usually fairly short and covers basic concepts about the methodology. Green belt exams are longer and can include statistics questions and some basic calculations. Black belt exams often take up to four hours to complete; they test understanding and application. The exams may include difficult statistical problems or questions about how a project leader would handle various situations. Although exams vary by organization, this book was built around the body-of-knowledge requirements published by the Council for Six Sigma Certification (CSSC).
